concept.name: Position sizing
concept.definition: The process of determining how large each trade or position should be — the 'how much' decision of a trading system — expressed as units, contracts, or the fraction of equity risked per trade. In the practitioner literature (Tharp) it is identified, rather than entry selection, as the dominant determinant of whether a system meets its objectives.
concept.intuition: Two traders running the identical profitable system can end with wildly different outcomes — one compounding steadily, one ruined — purely because of how much each risked per trade.
concept.mechanics: Given account equity, per-trade risk tolerance, and the trade's initial risk (stop distance times point value), compute the size so a stopped-out trade loses the intended fraction of equity. Models include percent risk (fixed fractional), percent volatility (ATR-based), fixed ratio, and Kelly-style fractions; aggregate caps such as daily loss limits sit on top.
concept.formula: Position size = (account equity * risk fraction) / (per-unit risk), where per-unit risk = |entry - stop| * value per point (per contract).
concept.failure_modes: Sizing rules calibrated on a historical R-multiple distribution fail when the regime shifts; percent-risk models suffer lot-rounding distortions on small accounts, and correlated simultaneous positions make aggregate risk far larger than per-trade math suggests.
concept.misconceptions: Position sizing cannot turn a negative-expectancy system into a winner — it only determines how the edge (or its absence) is expressed in the equity curve. Fixed lot sizes are not a neutral default: they break compounding and drawdown protection.
concept.example: With $50,000 equity, 1% risk per trade, and a 4-point stop worth $200 per contract, the percent-risk size is $500 / $200 = 2 contracts.

citations.source: Trade Loss Tracker: extended summary of Van K. Tharp, The Definitive Guide to Position Sizing Strategies
